doc.title: CDC to Iceberg through Debezium
doc.p: You capture changes from a MySQL or PostgreSQL database with Debezium and land them in Iceberg tables. The hard part is not the pipeline; it is knowing, column by column, what each MySQL type becomes on the way, and finding the inconsistencies in the source before they turn into broken or silently wrong data.
SchemaForge designs the Iceberg side from the source side, under rules, and shows every inconsistency first.

section.title: The idea
section.code: source schema ──► consistency check ──► pipeline (rules, Debezium's included) ──► Iceberg schema (MySQL or every problem shown every column mapped, decided once + mapping report + Debezium settings

list.item: The source follows the Debezium rule pack (rules.md), which a pipeline adds to it.
A pipeline links two schemas in SchemaForge: a MySQL or PostgreSQL source and an Iceberg target.

Each side has its own collection of rule packs: the source, its type's defaults and the Debezium pack; the target, Iceberg's defaults and whatever packs you add (SCD, star schema, your naming). It carries the rules for the mapping, including the Debezium rule pack's connector settings.
The Iceberg tables are generated from the source by those rules; you and the agent then refine them (partitions, sort orders, extra columns) like any schema.
When the source changes, the pipeline shows what the Iceberg side must do: an allowed schema evolution, or a change it cannot take, flagged.

section.title: Inconsistencies, shown first
section.p: Before anything is mapped, the source is checked. Every finding is marked on the tables and columns in every perspective, gathered in the Consistency perspective, and given to the agent with a suggested fix.

list.item: the same column, different types: customer_id int in one table, bigint in another
a relationship whose two ends differ: int referencing bigint, signed referencing unsigned
one kind of data in many types: money as decimal(10,2), decimal(12,2) and double
lengths that drift: email varchar(100) here, varchar(255) there
mixed character sets or collations across tables
DATETIME and TIMESTAMP both used for points in time (Debezium treats them differently, below)
TINYINT(1) used as a boolean in some tables and as a number in others

section.p: Hazards on the way to Iceberg through Debezium, from MySQL (PostgreSQL's are in the Debezium rule pack):

list.item: BIGINT UNSIGNED: Debezium's default (bigint.unsigned.handling.mode=long) silently corrupts values above 2^63 − 1; the safe choice is precise, giving decimal(20,0)
a table without a primary key: no identifier fields on the Iceberg side, so no upserts, only appends
zero dates (0000-00-00): become null for nullable columns and the epoch for NOT NULL ones
TIME values outside a day (MySQL allows up to 838 hours): only 00:00 to 23:59:59.999999 is captured correctly
ENUM and SET arrive as strings; their allowed values are lost unless kept (as a comment or a check)
FLOAT or DOUBLE for money
DECIMAL under decimal.handling.mode=double or string: precision lost or the type changed

section.title: How each MySQL type lands
section.p: With the Debezium rule pack's shipped defaults (below):

row.cell: float, double (flagged when the kind is money)
string, allowed values kept in the comment
string, or variant on format version 3
geometry on format version 3, else a struct

section.p: Every row is a rule: you can change any of them in the pipeline's rules, and the change shows at once on every table it affects.

section.title: How each PostgreSQL type lands
section.p: With the Debezium rule pack's shipped defaults:

row.cell: flagged: give it a precision and scale
float, double (flagged when the kind is money)
string, or variant on format version 3
string, allowed values kept in the comment

section.p: Arrays and partitioned tables (publish_via_partition_root) are still to be checked against Debezium's documentation before they are mapped.

section.title: Debezium's settings are rules
section.p: How types travel (decimal.handling.mode, bigint.unsigned.handling.mode, time.precision.mode, binary.handling.mode, the TinyInt-to-boolean converter, the zero-date fallback) is set in the Debezium rule pack (rules.md), in Standards, per template or per schema, like any other rule. The pipeline reads them, maps every column by them, and writes them out for the connector, so the two can never disagree. The type table above assumes the shipped defaults.

section.title: The Iceberg tables
section.p: Generated by the pipeline's rules, then refined with the agent:

list.item: identifier fields from the source's primary key, so changes are upserts; a table without one is flagged (append-only, or you choose a key)
merge-on-read for deletes, updates and merges, and format version 3, from the Iceberg defaults
partition spec and sort order from the rules (e.g. by day of a time column, sorted by the key)
CDC columns, if the rules ask for them, named by the naming rules: the operation (c, u, d, r), the event time, and the source position (binlog file and position, or GTID)
deletes: applied as deletes, or kept as rows marked deleted, as the rules say
relationships carried over as logical ones, so the diagram stays the same shape
the Iceberg schema, a normal SchemaForge schema
the mapping report: every source column, its Iceberg column, the rule that decided it, and every inconsistency and hazard with what was done about it
the Debezium settings for the connector (from the rule pack, plus the converter's column list)
the Iceberg DDL (Spark SQL, Trino) or table metadata, as for any Iceberg schema

section.title: When the source changes
section.p: A new locked version of the source schema is compared with what the pipeline last mapped:

list.item: additions (a new table, a new nullable column) map by the rules, as before
widenings Iceberg allows (int to long, float to double, a larger decimal precision) become schema evolution on the Iceberg table
anything else (a narrower type, a changed key, a dropped column the target still holds) is flagged with what it would break, for you to decide
